summary: Seasonal lag is the delay between peak insolation (solstices) and peak or minimum air temperature, caused largely by water's high latent heat and related to thermal inertia. The note explains how the lag length varies by climate, from 15-20 days in polar and continental areas to 2-3 months in oceanic locales, with examples such as San Francisco, East Asia and Eastern Canada. It also covers why equinoxes and solstices do not align with temperature, and notes that other planets show different lags, with Mars negligible and Venus and Mercury showing none.
one_line: Seasonal lag is the delay between solar insolation peaks and the warmest or coldest air temperatures, varying with climate and water influence.
key_facts: Seasonal lag is the delay of the date of maximum average air temperature until some time after the date of maximum insolation, the summer solstice.
Earth's seasonal lag is largely caused by the presence of large amounts of water, which has a high latent heat of freezing and of condensation.
Seasonal lag extremes range from 15–20 days for polar regions in summer and continental interiors such as Fairbanks, Alaska, to 2–3 months in oceanic locales.
In mid-latitude continental climates, seasonal lag is approximately 20–25 days in winter and 25–35 days in summer.
In most Northern Hemisphere regions, February is usually colder than November despite February having significantly later sunsets and more daylight overall.
San Francisco has an exceptionally long seasonal lag in summer, with average daily temperatures peaking in September, and very little seasonal lag in winter.
In Western Europe the seasonal lag is usually around a month.
In eastern Canada, February and August are the coldest and warmest months, respectively, because the seasonal lag is consistent in summer and winter.
Due to seasonal lag, the autumnal equinox (around September 22) is considerably warmer than the vernal equinox (around March 20) in most Northern Hemisphere regions.
Contrary to popular belief, there is no meteorological reason for designating the equinoxes and solstices as the first days of their respective seasons.
An analogous temperature lag occurs in diurnal variation, where maximum daily temperature occurs after noon.
Both seasonal and diurnal lag are manifestations of the general physical phenomenon of thermal inertia.
Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Saturn's moon Titan have substantial seasonal lags equivalent to between two and three months in Earth terms.
Mars has negligible seasonal lag of no more than a few days.
No seasonal lag would be detected on Venus or Mercury, which undergo no seasons in the sense used on Earth.
